extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative government scholars, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria about centralization vs. local (provincial) institutions and the defining characteristics and limits of judicial power in democratic republics. Useful for assessing institutional design, balance of powers, and civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between central government and central administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain interests are common to all parts of a nation... When the power which directs the general interests is centred in one place, or vested in the same persons, it constitutes a central government. In like manner the power of directing partial or local interests, when brought together into one place, constitutes what may be termed a central administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that central government (general interests) and central administration (local/partial interests) are distinct concepts which may coalesce but should be analytically separated when evaluating institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of combining centralized government and centralized administration
rubrics_metrics.description: When the power which directs the general interests is centred in one place, or vested in the same persons, it accustoms men to set their own will habitually and completely aside... Not only does this union of power subdue them compulsorily, but it affects them in the ordinary habits of life, and influences each individual, first separately and then collectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that uniting legislative/central authority with administrative centralization subdues civic initiative, diminishes public spirit, and creates dependence; use as a criterion against excessive concentration of both political and administrative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a powerful central government balanced against administrative centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot conceive that a nation can enjoy a secure or prosperous existence without a powerful centralization of government. But I am of opinion that a central administration enervates the nations in which it exists by incessantly diminishing their public spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design should accept some centralized governmental power for security/prosperity but avoid transferring detailed administrative control to the center; evaluate institutions for this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When vital, government should employ its own removable officers and rapid procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that, in whatever materially affects its existence, the Government should be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at pleasure, and accustomed to rapid methods of proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied recommendation (tax collection example): where state survival or major functions are at stake, prefer centralized, accountable, quickly-acting administrative agents rather than slow, dispersed local mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local administration can impede execution of national undertakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain undertakings are of importance to the whole State; but they cannot be put in execution, because there is no national administration to direct them. Abandoned to the exertions of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no durable benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as evaluative criterion: assess whether important national initiatives are feasible under a decentralized system; consider oversight mechanisms (e.g., state inspection or agents to prosecute local misdemeanors) to ensure uniform execution without destroying local independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central authority better than locals only when center is enlightened and locals ignorant
rubrics_metrics.description: The partisans of centralization... maintain that the Government directs the affairs of each locality better than the citizens could do it for themselves; this may be true when the central power is enlightened, and when the local districts are ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for subsidiarity: favor central intervention only if the central authority is demonstrably more knowledgeable/effective than local actors; otherwise, local collective strength will better serve public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization excels at routine prevention but fails at mobilizing free citizen cooperation for action
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization imparts without difficulty an admirable regularity to the routine of business... in short, it excels more in prevention than in action. Its force deserts it when society is to be disturbed or accelerated in its course; and if once the co-operation of private citizens is necessary to the furtherance of its measures, the secret of its impotence is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutional design, recognize centralization's comparative advantage in uniform routine enforcement and prevention, and its comparative disadvantage for dynamic, participatory, or rapidly adaptive collective actions requiring free citizen initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and indispensability of provincial (local) institutions in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe that provincial institutions are useful to all nations, but nowhere do they appear to me to be more indispensable than amongst a democratic people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: democratic polities should cultivate and preserve local/provincial institutions as training grounds for civic responsibility and as bulwarks against both mob rule and centralized despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of democracies concentrating power in the representative body
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the Government in the hands of the only power which directly represents the people... But when the same power is already in possession of all the attributes of the Government, it can scarcely refrain from penetrating into the details of the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as warning: evaluate democratic constitutions and practices for mechanisms preventing the single popularly-elected body from usurping administrative details and aggregating unchecked power (historical example: French Revolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen initiative and private undertakings as cumulative public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: When a private individual meditates an undertaking... he publishes his plan, offers to execute it himself, courts the assistance of other individuals... the sum of these private undertakings far exceeds all that the Government could have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for assessing social welfare and public goods provision: measure the extent to which institutions encourage decentralized private initiative and voluntary cooperation as complements or alternatives to state provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local administrative accessibility reduces jealousy and encourages civic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: As the administrative authority is within the reach of the citizens... it excites neither their jealousy nor their hatred; as its resources are limited, every one feels that he must not rely solely on its assistance... the duties of the private citizens are not supposed to have lapsed because the State assists in their fulfilment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether administrative structures are accessible and limited in scope so citizens remain engaged and feel compelled to participate rather than defer entirely to state actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of citizens in law enforcement and maintenance of order
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminal police of the United States cannot be compared to that of France... Nevertheless in no country does crime more rarely elude punishment. The reason is, that every one conceives himself to be interested in furnishing evidence of the act committed, and in stopping the delinquent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for fostering public-spirited participation in policing (e.g., committees, local reporting), particularly where centralized police capacity is limited; civic engagement can substitute for expansive coercive apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of judicial power — (1) duty of arbitration (only when rights contested)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But rights must be contested in order to warrant the interference of a tribunal; and an action must be brought to obtain the decision of a judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for judicial role: judges should confine themselves to resolving actual disputes brought before them, not acting proactively or on abstract questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of judicial power — (2) pronounces on special cases, not on general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The second characteristic of judicial power is that it pronounces on special cases, and not upon general principles. If a judge in deciding a particular point destroys a general principle... he remains within the ordinary limits of his functions. But if he directly attacks a general principle without having a particular case in view, he leaves the circle...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate judicial behavior by whether decisions arise from concrete cases and avoid issuing abstract, general pronouncements outside dispute contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of judicial power — (3) passive nature: cannot act unless appealed to
rubrics_metrics.description: The third characteristic of the judicial power is its inability to act unless it is appealed to... The judicial power is by its nature devoid of action; it must be put in motion in order to produce a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial institutions should be assessed for respect of passivity: they should not initiate prosecutions, hunt out wrongs, or usurp censorship of laws absent proper cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: American judicial right to base decisions on the constitution (judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have acknowledged the right of the judges to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws. In other words, they have left them at liberty not to apply such laws as may appear to them to be unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a distinct institutional principle: courts may refuse to apply statutes conflicting with the constitution; evaluate presence, scope, and acceptance of judicial review in a polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional supremacy with an amendment mechanism as check on judicial power
rubrics_metrics.description: An American constitution... constitutes a detached whole, which, as it represents the determination of the whole people, is no less binding on the legislator than on the private citizen, but which may be altered by the will of the people in predetermined cases, according to established rules... the nation can always reduce its magistrates to obedience by changing its constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the safety of judicial review, consider whether the constitution has a democratic amendment path that keeps judges accountable and prevents judicial supremacy over the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicial usurpation in other systems (comparative caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in France the tribunals were authorized to disobey the laws on the ground of their being opposed to the constitution, the supreme power would in fact be placed in their hands... It would be still more unreasonable to invest the English judges with the right of resisting the decisions of the legislative body, since the Parliament which makes the laws also makes the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative standard: evaluate the interplay of judicial authority and constitutional theory (immutable constitution vs. parliamentary sovereignty) to predict risks of judicial usurpation or legislative omnipotence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of durable public motivation: patriotism and religion over mere law
rubrics_metrics.description: Patriotism and religion are the only two motives in the world which can permanently direct the whole of a body politic to one end. Laws cannot succeed in rekindling the ardor of an extinguished faith, but men may be interested in the fate of their country by the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional designs and civic education for their capacity to connect laws and public life to deeper motives (patriotism, religion, civic sentiment) to sustain long-run public cooperation beyond legal compulsion.
